sections.text: Compound interest grows money in doublings, and the Rule of 72 is a mental shortcut for how often they happen: divide 72 by the annual rate in percent to estimate the years to double. At 6% that gives 12 years, and the exact answer is 11.90. The shortcut is very good between about 4% and 10% and drifts at the extremes. This post uses exact calculations to show where the rule works, where it fails, and what matters more for growth: time or rate. All growth rates here are assumptions for illustration, and past performance does not guarantee future results.
How the rule works and how accurate it is

With annual compounding, the exact doubling time is ln(2) / ln(1 + r). For small rates, ln(1 + r) is close to r, which gives 69.3 / r. The number 72 is used because it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12 and sits closer to the exact answer for rates around 8%. The table compares the rule with the exact time for annual compounding and for monthly compounding.

The rule is within 3% of the exact figure from 2% to 12% and within 7% at 24%. It also works in reverse: to double in 10 years you need 72 / 10 = 7.2%, and the exact annual rate is 7.18%. The same shortcut applies to debt. A balance on a 24% card that is left alone doubles in about 3 years under the rule, and the exact figure is 3.22 years with annual compounding or 2.92 with monthly compounding.
Using doublings to project a balance
Doublings turn long horizons into small arithmetic. At 7%, the exact doubling time is 10.24 years, and the rule says 10.29. A single $10,000 deposit grows like this with annual compounding:

Rounding the doubling time to exactly 10 years would suggest four doublings and 16x, which overstates. Using the rule (72 divided by 7, about 10.29 years) gives about 3.89 doublings, or 14.81x, close to the exact 14.97x. Note how late the growth arrives. The first ten years add $9,672, while the last ten add $73,622, 52.7% of all the growth over 40 years. That back-loading is the real argument for starting early, and for not stopping.

These are $10,000 lump sums compounded annually. Starting from 6% for 20 years ($32,071), adding ten years multiplies the result by 1.79, while adding two percentage points of return multiplies it by 1.45. To reach the 8% result of $46,610 at 6%, you need 26.4 years instead of 20. Time and rate both matter, but a decade of time is worth more than two points of rate in this range. Rate is also the part you control least. You cannot choose the return, though you can choose costs: a fee that takes 1 point of a 7% return leaves 6%, and over 30 years $10,000 becomes $57,435 instead of $76,123, about 25% less. Doubling time changes from 10.24 years to 11.90.

Somewhat, but less than rate or time. On $10,000 at 7% for 30 years, annual compounding gives $76,123, quarterly $80,192, monthly $81,165 and daily $81,645. Going from annual to monthly adds 6.6%, and from monthly to daily only 0.6%. The frequency that applies to you is set by the account or investment, so compare accounts on their stated annual yield rather than guessing.

Prices rise too, so a 7% nominal return does not double your buying power in 10 years. If inflation is 3%, an assumption, the real return is (1.07 / 1.03) - 1 = 3.88%, and the real doubling time is 18.19 years. Rule of 72 with 4% gives 18, a good estimate. Use a real return when asking what a balance will buy.

items: Using the rule with rates above about 20% or below 1%, where error grows. Compute exactly in those cases.
Treating a long-run average as a yearly guarantee. Real returns vary, and a bad early year can matter.
Forgetting fees and taxes, which reduce the net rate that compounds.
Counting doublings without checking whether you add or withdraw money, which changes the path. The Compound Interest Calculator handles regular contributions.
Assuming that starting late means giving up. Higher contributions and more years still help; the tables show the cost of waiting, not that growth stops.

sections.text: Where the Rule of 72 does not apply

The rule assumes one fixed rate and no deposits or withdrawals. It does not describe variable returns, regular contributions, taxes, or fees that change the rate. It is for rough checking, not planning. Enter your own deposit, contribution, rate and years into the Compound Interest Calculator for a precise projection, and use conservative rates.
